Published: 2026-10-03 · Updated: 2026-10-09

Industrial guide · Physical and environmental diligence

# Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental

This guide organizes the physical, environmental, title, survey, zoning, lease, and utility questions that commonly affect industrial property acquisitions across the nine Illinois counties covered by these guides.

Educational, not legal, environmental, engineering, or investment advice.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

## In brief

- Industrial diligence is different because prior uses, heavy systems, loading, utilities, and environmental history can drive value and closing risk.
- The purchase agreement should control deadlines, access, seller deliverables, and remedies for findings.
- Environmental review often starts with a Phase I ESA and may expand to sampling, vapor, tanks, asbestos, lead, or regulatory closure issues.
- Physical diligence should convert roof, slab, dock, utility, fire-protection, pavement, and drainage findings into a capital plan.
- Findings usually become a decision about price, credits, escrows, repairs, insurance, indemnities, or whether to proceed.
- Owner lens: For an owner, diligence is also the start of the permanent building file. Preserve reports, permits, warranties, maintenance logs, environmental records, and repair decisions for lenders, insurers, tenants, and a future buyer.

_A renovation inspection in Vicenza, Italy. Use qualified professionals to document building systems and property specific findings._

## Why industrial diligence is different

Industrial property diligence is not limited to rent, taxes, and a walk-through. Past and current operations may involve chemicals, fuels, tanks, floor drains, heavy equipment, vehicle repair, food handling, manufacturing residues, or unusual utility loads.

Physical systems also carry deal risk. A roof, slab, dock package, sprinkler system, transformer, truck court, or drainage problem can change occupancy timing and capital needs.

For a broader acquisition framework, see the investment diligence guide . For building-fit questions, use the industrial evaluation checklist and the building types and specifications guide .

## Organizing the diligence period

The purchase and sale agreement should state when the diligence period starts, what the seller must deliver, what access is allowed, and what happens if the buyer objects. Calendar every notice date before ordering reports.

Access needs should be specific. Environmental consultants, roofers, surveyors, engineers, lenders, insurers, contractors, appraisers, and utility representatives may need different site visits, tenant coordination, and sampling permissions.

Sellers can reduce friction by pre-assembling the documents listed in the selling guide . A clean file does not replace diligence, but it helps buyers and lenders ask better questions.

- Use a diligence tracker with document status, responsible party, deadline, and open issue.
- Require insurance, safety rules, and escort procedures for invasive or operationally sensitive inspections.
- Coordinate tenant notices and quiet-hours if the property is occupied.
- Reserve enough time for follow-up testing when the initial report identifies a concern.

## Environmental diligence

Environmental work is usually scoped by the property history, intended use, lender requirements, and the buyer's risk tolerance. The consultant and legal counsel should explain the standard, reliance language, and any data gaps.

### Phase I ESA and AAI

A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment is commonly prepared under ASTM E1527-21 and federal All Appropriate Inquiries concepts. The U.S. EPA All Appropriate Inquiries page explains the federal framework and links to current rules.

The scope commonly includes records review, historical sources, site reconnaissance, interviews, and a report identifying recognized environmental conditions. The user also has responsibilities, such as providing specialized knowledge, commonly known information, and information about purchase price or environmental liens when applicable.

AAI has timing rules: the inquiry must be conducted or updated within one year before acquisition, and certain components must be conducted or updated within 180 days. Confirm current requirements and reliance language with the environmental consultant and counsel.

### RECs, HRECs, and CRECs

A recognized environmental condition, or REC, points to a likely presence or release of hazardous substances or petroleum products. A historical recognized environmental condition, or HREC, generally indicates a past release that has been addressed to the applicable standard.

A controlled recognized environmental condition, or CREC, generally means a past release remains subject to controls, restrictions, or ongoing obligations. The words matter because they can affect lender review, buyer obligations, and future use.

### Phase II sampling and vapor intrusion

A Phase II investigation may include soil, groundwater, soil-gas, indoor air, or other sampling. The purpose is to test specific concerns, not to prove that no risk exists anywhere on the property.

Vapor intrusion review can be important where volatile chemicals or petroleum releases may migrate into buildings. Sampling methods, seasonal conditions, building pressure, and mitigation design should be handled by qualified environmental professionals.

### Asbestos, lead, PCBs, USTs, and other regulated materials

Older industrial buildings may require separate review for asbestos-containing materials, lead-based paint, PCBs in equipment or caulk, underground storage tanks, aboveground tanks, hydraulic lifts, sumps, and floor drains. These are often outside a basic Phase I scope unless specifically added.

Ask whether the consultant recommends targeted surveys before demolition, renovation, financing, or occupancy. Removal and disposal rules can affect timing and cost.

### Illinois EPA SRP and NFR letters

The Illinois EPA Site Remediation Program is a voluntary cleanup program that can lead to a No Further Remediation letter for addressed conditions. An NFR letter is not the same as saying every environmental risk is gone.

Review the recorded terms, institutional controls, engineered barriers, exposure routes, and future-use limits. Counsel and the consultant should confirm whether the proposed use remains consistent with the closure.

### Landowner liability protections

Federal landowner liability protections are concept-based and fact-specific. They may depend on proper AAI, continuing obligations, no affiliation issues, and conduct after acquisition.

Do not treat a report alone as a guarantee. Review the facts with environmental counsel before relying on any protection.

## Physical diligence

Physical diligence should identify current condition, code or safety concerns, near-term repairs, long-term capital needs, and operational constraints. A property condition assessment may reference ASTM E2018 concepts through ASTM , but the scope should match the asset and the deal.

### Roof, structure, and slab

Review roof age, membrane type, warranty, leaks, drainage, penetrations, insulation, repairs, and replacement timing. For structure and slab, inspect settlement, cracking, joints, floor flatness, load capacity, mezzanines, roof framing, and signs of impact or water intrusion.

### Docks, doors, and equipment

Dock levelers, bumpers, seals, shelters, overhead doors, drive-in doors, controls, and restraints affect safety and operations. Field-test condition where practical and compare the loading package to the intended use.

Compare the actual fleet to gates, docks, truck courts, and overhead obstructions using the vehicle dimensions and turning-path reference . Have a qualified engineer review swept paths and required operational margins; cargo-box dimensions alone do not establish site access.

### Mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing review should cover remaining useful life, capacity, code concerns, maintenance records, and tenant-specific modifications. Electrical capacity should be confirmed against panels, service, transformer, utility data, and equipment requirements.

For fire protection, ask for sprinkler inspection reports, alarm records, deficiencies, hydraulic calculations, fire-pump tests if applicable, and any storage or commodity assumptions. Verify sprinkler design with a fire-protection engineer, insurer, and authority having jurisdiction.

### Pavement, drainage, and flood

Pavement matters for trailers, forklifts, snow removal, drainage, and yard use. Inspect asphalt, concrete, catch basins, detention, ponding, striping, curbs, and truck-wear areas.

Flood and drainage review should include local records and the FEMA Flood Map Service Center . FEMA mapping does not replace a civil engineer's review of site drainage or stormwater obligations.

### Accessibility, elevators, and cranes

Accessibility review should consider parking, routes, entrances, restrooms, office areas, signage, and any alterations. Elevators, hoists, cranes, bridge cranes, and jib cranes require records, load ratings, inspections, service contracts, and ownership clarification.

### Deferred maintenance and capital plan

Convert inspection notes into a capital plan with timing, cost ranges, responsible party, and business impact. Separate immediate life-safety items from monitor-and-maintain items and future improvements.

## Title, survey, and land

Title and survey review connects legal rights to physical use. The title commitment lists requirements and exceptions; the ALTA survey helps show boundaries, easements, improvements, access, and encroachments.

Review access rights, shared drive agreements, cross-parking, utilities, drainage easements, signage rights, recorded covenants, and any reciprocal easement agreements. A truck entrance that crosses another parcel needs documented rights, not just historical use.

For rail-served property, confirm rail agreements, switch rights, track maintenance, active service, clearance, and whether the railroad or a third party controls access. Rail value can disappear if the legal and physical service rights do not match the marketing description.

## Zoning and permits

Zoning diligence should confirm the current district, permitted uses, special uses, variances, nonconforming rights, outdoor storage, parking, truck routing, screening, signage, and hours of operation. A zoning verification letter can help document how the municipality views the property.

Permits and certificates of occupancy show whether past work and uses were approved. Check for open permits, violations, expired approvals, fire-code issues, unpermitted mezzanines, and tenant improvements that may need closeout.

For local research starting points, use the nine-county hub and municipal records. For Chicago-specific research, see the Chicago commercial real estate guide .

## Operational and lease diligence for leased industrial

Lease diligence should test whether the income, obligations, and operational rights shown in the rent roll are supported by signed documents. Request every lease, amendment, guaranty, side letter, estoppel, SNDA, and notice relevant to occupancy.

- Estoppels: confirm rent, term, deposits, defaults, options, exclusive rights, and tenant claims.
- SNDAs: coordinate lender, buyer, and tenant rights after a foreclosure or ownership change.
- CAM reconciliations: test recoveries, caps, exclusions, reserves, management fees, and year-end balances.
- Repair obligations: identify who pays for roof, structure, HVAC, pavement, dock equipment, fire protection, and capital replacements.
- Hazardous materials clauses: compare lease rights to actual operations, permits, storage, and environmental reports.
- Parking and trailer rights: confirm allocated spaces, yard rights, storage limits, and rules for containers or fleet vehicles.

The commercial leasing guide explains why lease labels do not replace a clause-by-clause review.

## Utilities and infrastructure

Industrial users often need utility confirmation before they can commit. Electricity, gas, water, sanitary sewer, storm sewer, compressed air, fiber, and telecom should be reviewed against the user's equipment and occupancy schedule.

For much of the region, electrical capacity questions may involve ComEd , the serving utility, an electrical engineer, and the tenant's equipment vendor. Confirm service voltage, phase, amperage, transformer ownership, spare capacity, upgrade lead times, and shutdown requirements.

For existing or proposed battery energy storage, collect ownership and service contracts, approved plans, utility permissions, commissioning records, safety documentation and removal obligations. The BESS owner guide explains storage, peak savings, engineered backup, fire and insurance review, and standalone storage land leases. Neither a large service nor nearby transmission guarantees interconnection capacity.

Gas, water, and sewer review should include meter size, pressure, discharge limits, floor drains, pretreatment, process water, fire flow, and municipal capacity. Fiber and telecom are separate from an address being generally serviceable.

## Turning findings into price, credits, escrows, or repairs

Diligence findings are useful only when they lead to a clear decision. The buyer can accept the risk, renegotiate price, request a credit, create an escrow, require seller repairs, modify representations, obtain insurance, or terminate if the contract allows.

Sellers should distinguish between documented defects, buyer preferences, and speculative future upgrades. Buyers should distinguish between ordinary maintenance and issues that change value, financing, insurability, or lawful use.

Material findings should be tied to evidence: report page, photo, contractor proposal, municipal response, title exception, lease clause, or consultant memo. That keeps negotiations focused on facts.

## Diligence checklist

This checklist is a starting point. The actual scope should match the property type, contract, lender, tenant, intended use, and risk tolerance.

**Industrial property diligence checklist**
- Item: Purpose: Typical provider
- Phase I ESA / AAI: Review historical and current environmental risk and support liability-protection analysis.: Environmental consultant and environmental counsel.
- Phase II or targeted sampling: Test specific concerns from records, site conditions, or Phase I findings.: Environmental consultant and laboratory.
- Asbestos, lead, PCB, tank, and regulated-material surveys: Identify special handling, renovation, demolition, or closure issues.: Specialty environmental consultant.
- Property condition assessment: Evaluate building systems, immediate repairs, and capital needs.: Engineer, architect, or PCA consultant.
- Roof report: Assess roof condition, leaks, warranty, drainage, and replacement timing.: Roof consultant or qualified contractor.
- Structural and slab review: Confirm load, cracking, settlement, mezzanines, cranes, and equipment impacts.: Structural engineer.
- MEP review: Confirm capacity, useful life, code concerns, and maintenance requirements.: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing contractors or engineers.
- Fire-protection review: Confirm inspections, deficiencies, design assumptions, and storage compatibility.: Fire-protection contractor, engineer, insurer, and AHJ.
- Pavement and drainage review: Evaluate truck areas, ponding, stormwater, catch basins, and yard surface.: Civil engineer or pavement consultant.
- Title commitment and exception documents: Identify liens, requirements, easements, covenants, and recorded restrictions.: Title company and real estate attorney.
- Survey: Show boundaries, improvements, access, encroachments, easements, and parking or yard layout.: Licensed surveyor.
- Zoning verification: Confirm permitted use, nonconforming rights, parking, outdoor storage, and open violations.: Municipality, zoning consultant, and land-use attorney.
- Lease and tenant file review: Confirm rent, term, options, obligations, recoveries, defaults, and use rights.: Real estate attorney, broker, property manager, and buyer.
- Utility confirmation: Verify electric, gas, water, sewer, fire flow, and communication service for the intended use.: Utilities, engineers, contractors, and tenant equipment vendors.
- Capital plan and negotiation summary: Translate findings into price, credit, escrow, repair, insurance, or closing decisions.: Buyer, broker, counsel, lender, consultants, and seller.

For terminology, the Phase I ESA / AAI , ALTA survey , and title commitment glossary entries provide plain-English definitions.

> This guide is general education, not engineering, environmental, legal, tax, appraisal, brokerage, or investment advice. Verify environmental conditions, building systems, title, survey, zoning, leases, utilities, and transaction decisions with qualified professionals before acting.

## Continue with the owner guides

For the operating and financial questions behind this decision:
- Commercial property insurance: an owner renewal checklist
- How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building
- How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?

Market orientation · Illinois logistics corridors

# Chicagoland industrial submarkets and logistics corridors

A geography-first orientation to industrial clusters, freight infrastructure, and location diligence across the Illinois counties around Chicago.

No rent, vacancy, pricing, or ranking claims.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

## In brief
- Submarket names are brokerage conventions, not legal boundaries.
- Always verify the parcel’s municipality, county, zoning, truck routes, utilities, and tax district.
- Corridors often follow interstate, tollway, airport, rail, and intermodal access.
- Aurora, Elgin, Joliet, and other municipalities can cross county lines, so county assumptions must be checked.
- This guide describes geography and infrastructure only; it does not rank submarkets or state market statistics.
- Owner lens: For an owner planning to lease or sell later, test actual staff and shipment routes and the pool of replacement users, not just distance to an interstate, airport, or terminal.

_The BNSF intermodal terminal in Cicero, Illinois. Freight connections matter, but verify each property’s actual routes and site access._

## How to use submarket labels

Industrial submarket names are shorthand. They help brokers, lenders, owners, and tenants talk about geography, but they are not zoning districts, tax districts, or municipal boundaries. A data provider may draw “O’Hare,” “I-55,” or “Joliet” differently from a broker or municipality.

Before underwriting a 10,000 to 100,000 square foot building, verify the parcel’s county and municipality using the nine-county industrial research hub . Then match the address to zoning, permitted use, truck routes, taxes, and utilities. A building can be marketed under one corridor name while legally sitting in a different taxing body or approval jurisdiction.

### Practical use

Use labels for search and tours; use legal records for closing, financing, zoning, environmental review, and municipal approvals.

## Corridors and clusters described by geography

### O?Hare corridor

Elk Grove Village, Bensenville, Wood Dale, Franklin Park, Schiller Park, and Des Plaines are tied to I-90, I-294, I-190, and O?Hare air cargo. Verify county, municipality, truck circulation, and airport-adjacent restrictions.

### North Cook and Lake County

Northbrook, Wheeling, Buffalo Grove, Lincolnshire, Libertyville, Gurnee, and Waukegan relate to I-94, US-41, and local arterials. Lake County means Illinois, not Indiana.

### Northwest and I-90

Schaumburg, Hoffman Estates, Elgin, Huntley, and the Belvidere direction follow I-90. Boone County is outside scope, and Elgin crosses county lines.

### Central DuPage, I-355 and I-88

Addison, Carol Stream, West Chicago, Glendale Heights, Lombard, Naperville, and Aurora relate to I-355, I-88, North Avenue, Roosevelt Road, and DuPage Airport. Aurora and Naperville cross county lines.

### West Cook, I-290 and inner I-55

Bedford Park, McCook, Hodgkins, Cicero, Bellwood, Melrose Park, and Northlake form an infill logistics belt near BNSF Cicero, CSX Bedford Park, and Union Pacific Global 2.

### I-55 corridor

Bolingbrook, Romeoville, Woodridge, Lemont, and Plainfield are commonly grouped along I-55, I-355, and nearby arterials across Will, DuPage, and Cook County.

### I-80 and Joliet area

Joliet, Elwood, Channahon, Minooka, Shorewood, University Park, and Monee are oriented to I-80 and I-55. BNSF Logistics Park Chicago and Union Pacific Global 4 are key reference points.

### South Cook, I-57 and I-294

Alsip, Bridgeview, Chicago Heights, Harvey, Markham, Matteson, and South Holland sit near I-57, I-294, I-80, and Calumet-area rail infrastructure, including Norfolk Southern, CN, and other rail references.

### City of Chicago industrial corridors

The City of Chicago uses official industrial corridor planning and Planned Manufacturing District tools. See the Industrial Corridor Modernization Initiative .

### Kane, Kendall, DeKalb, McHenry, and Grundy outer markets

Aurora, Batavia, Geneva, St. Charles, Yorkville, Oswego, Plano, DeKalb, Sycamore, Woodstock, Crystal Lake, and Morris are smaller clusters tied to I-88, the I-39 direction, and I-80 west.

## Freight infrastructure overview

Freight infrastructure should be treated as a location attribute, not a guarantee. A building can be near a terminal or airport and still have poor truck access, wrong zoning, inadequate loading, or limited yard depth.

### Intermodal terminals and rail references

**Selected Chicago-area freight facilities to verify with official railroad sources**
- Facility: Railroad: Municipality or area: County: Official source
- Cicero Intermodal: BNSF: Cicero: Cook: BNSF facility listings
- Logistics Park Chicago: BNSF: Elwood: Will: BNSF facility listing
- Global 2: Union Pacific: Northlake: Cook: Union Pacific Global 2
- Global 4: Union Pacific: Joliet: Will: Union Pacific Global 4
- Bedford Park Intermodal: CSX: Bedford Park: Cook: CSX intermodal
- Landers: Norfolk Southern: Chicago: Cook: Norfolk Southern
- Chicago/Harvey terminal: CN: Harvey area: Cook: CN intermodal terminals

### Airports, interstates and tollways

**Air and highway references for industrial location review**
- Category: Examples: Source to check
- Air cargo: O’Hare cargo; Midway for airport adjacency; Chicago Rockford as a regional cargo point outside the nine-county scope.: FlyChicago cargo
- Tollways: I-90, I-294, I-355, I-88, and other Illinois Tollway facilities.: Illinois Tollway
- State and interstate routes: I-55, I-57, I-80, I-39 direction, US-41, and state-maintained arterials.: Illinois Department of Transportation

## How location factors enter underwriting

For 10,000 to 100,000 square foot industrial buildings, location underwriting is usually specific and practical. A small user or private investor cares about the actual drive, dock, labor, and approval path more than a broad corridor label.

### Factors to test
- Labor access: shift timing, transit availability, parking, and commute patterns.
- Truck routes: municipal restrictions, bridge clearances, road weight limits, turning movements, and neighborhood constraints.
- Last-mile versus regional distribution: customer proximity, expressway access, driver hours, and delivery window reliability.
- Tollway costs: repeated toll exposure can affect operating cost even when the route is efficient.
- Building function: clear height, loading, truck court, yard, power, sprinklers, office ratio, and expansion area. See the industrial building guide .

Nearby infrastructure does not replace property-level diligence. A building can sit near I-55 and still have a difficult left turn, shallow dock apron, or ordinance that limits trailer storage.

## Verification steps before relying on a submarket

Use this sequence before marketing a building, signing an LOI, or budgeting improvements.

### Checklist
- Confirm the address, PIN, county, municipality, township, school district, and fire district in the county hub .
- Verify zoning, legal nonconforming status, outdoor storage, parking, truck routes, and hours of operation with the municipality.
- Review utilities: electric service, gas, water, sanitary, stormwater, fire protection, and available capacity.
- Check access: curb cuts, easements, shared drives, rail rights, signal timing, bridge limits, and municipal truck-route maps.
- Compare the building to the user need: loading, clear height, power, office finish, yard, floor condition, and expansion land.
- Review taxes, incentives, TIFs, enterprise zones, and transfer taxes with the Illinois industrial property tax guide .

## Sources

These links are starting points for official verification. Use parcel, terminal, airport, tollway, and municipal sources together.

### Official and operator sources
- City of Chicago Industrial Corridor Modernization Initiative
- Chicago Department of Aviation cargo information
- BNSF facility listings
- Union Pacific Global 2 and Union Pacific Global 4
- CSX intermodal , Norfolk Southern , and CN intermodal terminals
- Illinois Tollway and Illinois Department of Transportation

For sale, lease, or investment context, cross-check selling industrial property , commercial leasing , commercial investment , and the glossary .

> This guide is general education, not legal, zoning, engineering, environmental, logistics, appraisal, brokerage, or investment advice. Submarket labels and freight references change by source and project. Verify jurisdiction, zoning, truck routes, utilities, tax records, incentives, and infrastructure access with official offices and qualified professionals before acting.

Illinois, USA · County-by-county research

# Chicagoland industrial real estate: nine Illinois counties

Use this regional hub to investigate warehouse, distribution, manufacturing, and flex property in Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry, and Will counties. Start with the parcel and the operation, then identify the authority and records that actually apply.

Educational research, not listings or current market statistics.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

## In brief

- Covers nine Illinois counties: Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry, and Will.
- Confirm the county, the municipality or unincorporated status, and every PIN first. Authority follows the parcel.
- Each county section links the official planning, zoning, parcel, and assessment offices.
- Aurora, Elgin, and Joliet cross county lines; Lake County here means Illinois, not Indiana.
- Owner lens: A sale or expansion can involve separate municipal, county, fire, utility, stormwater, and tax reviews. Confirm parcel boundaries, service providers, and responsibility for each approval before committing capital.

> Defined scope. This guide covers these nine counties in Illinois, USA. It is not an exhaustive or official definition of “Chicagoland.” Indiana and Wisconsin properties are outside this guide; Lake County here means Lake County, Illinois, not Lake County, Indiana.

_Small- and mid-bay industrial buildings in Elk Grove Village, in Cook and DuPage counties, typical of the 10,000 to 100,000 SF segment._

## Establish jurisdiction before comparing locations

Record the street address, every property index number (PIN), county, and incorporated municipality or unincorporated status. A postal city, listing label, or county tax record does not establish the zoning authority. Municipalities can cross county lines, and a project can involve several parcels. Check each parcel rather than assigning the whole site from one address.

For property inside a city or village, start with its planning, zoning, and building staff. For unincorporated property, start with the county department linked below. Confirm any shared-service arrangement and separate fire, health, highway, utility, or stormwater approvals. County assessment and mapping resources can be useful even where municipal zoning applies.

Use GIS as a research aid, not a survey, title opinion, zoning approval, or guarantee of utility service. A comprehensive plan describes policy or future land use; it is not the same as today's zoning or permission to operate. Municipal examples below are orientation points, not recommendations or assurances that industrial space is available.

### County assessment offices

Cook County has an elected county assessor. In the other eight counties, township assessors typically set initial values and the county supervisor of assessments or chief county assessment officer supervises, equalizes, and publishes them. Start with the county office below to identify parcels, assessment history, exemptions, and appeal deadlines; verify tax bills with the county treasurer separately.

**Official assessment offices for the nine counties**
- County: Office
- Cook: Cook County Assessor
- DeKalb: DeKalb County Assessment Office (Chief County Assessment Officer)
- DuPage: DuPage County Supervisor of Assessments
- Grundy: Grundy County Supervisor of Assessments
- Kane: Kane County Supervisor of Assessments
- Kendall: Kendall County Supervisor of Assessments
- Lake: Lake County, Illinois Chief County Assessment Office
- McHenry: McHenry County Office of Assessments
- Will: Will County Supervisor of Assessments

## Cook County: distinguish Chicago from suburban authority

Chicago and suburban locations such as Bedford Park require separate local research. Chicago's zoning map and Department of Buildings are city resources, not countywide permitting systems. Cook County Building and Zoning directs incorporated-property inquiries to the applicable municipality and handles unincorporated areas, with a separate role for Forest Preserve property.

For a city distribution or service operation, trace the final approach from the public road to the loading area: curb access, backing movements, delivery windows, pedestrian conflicts, and any street-use requirements. For a suburban yard or warehouse, ask about outdoor storage and trailer parking independently of indoor warehouse permission. Neither a Chicago mailing address nor an industrial tax classification resolves those questions.

- Cook County Building and Zoning : county jurisdiction and building/zoning services.
- Cook County Assessor : identify parcels and assessment records; verify tax bills separately.
- Chicago zoning map and Chicago Department of Buildings : city-specific starting points.

## DeKalb County: separate mapped land use from approvals

DeKalb and Sycamore provide municipal starting points; sites outside municipal limits require county confirmation. DeKalb County Community Development reviews construction in unincorporated areas and administers county planning, zoning, subdivision, and stormwater regulations.

The county's Property Data and Maps page separates parcel information from Community Development mapping. Use those resources together to identify the site and inspect zoning and development layers. A mapped enterprise zone or a future-use designation does not by itself establish incentive eligibility or an approved industrial operation.

For a new manufacturing site or warehouse expansion, define the construction footprint, process-water needs, electrical loads, drainage changes, and required access before an approval discussion. Ask the responsible authority and utilities what can be served at this specific parcel; nearby development is not evidence that capacity is reserved for the project.

- DeKalb County Assessment Office : parcel identification, assessment records, and appeal information.
- DeKalb County Community Development : planning, building, and land-use responsibilities.
- DeKalb County Property Data and Maps : parcel, tax, land-record, and Community Development map entry points.

## DuPage County: reconcile municipal limits and building fit

Addison and Carol Stream are examples of DuPage County municipalities to research through their own departments. DuPage County Building and Zoning provides building permitting for unincorporated areas. Its Interactive Map Gallery links a parcel viewer for locating and checking the parcels under review.

For an existing warehouse or office/industrial flex building, compare the proposed office, storage, and production mix with the approved occupancy and required parking. Document whether a conversion changes fire separation, accessibility, ventilation, or loading needs. A flexible floor plan does not necessarily mean every activity is allowed.

Plot the actual lot, driveway, truck court, and easements before assuming there is room for more docks or trailer storage. When comparing a DuPage site with a neighboring-county option, keep the parcel and permitting records separate even if both share a familiar municipal or corridor label.

- DuPage County Supervisor of Assessments : assessment records, exemptions, and appeal procedures.
- DuPage County Building and Zoning : building, zoning, and planning services.
- DuPage County Interactive Map Gallery : county maps and the linked Parcel Viewer.

## Grundy County: investigate site development and approval paths

Morris is a municipal starting point within Grundy County. For a county-administered site, the Land Use Department separates Building, Planning and Zoning, and Environmental and Resource Conservation functions. Contact the right office for the proposed work rather than treating a zoning inquiry as a complete development review.

The Planning and Zoning Office describes hearings for map amendments, subdivision plats, special uses, and variances. Its page distinguishes recommendations to committees and the County Board from variance decisions by the Zoning Board of Appeals. If an industrial project needs relief or rezoning, confirm the applicable sequence before committing to a possession or construction date.

For a distribution yard or undeveloped manufacturing site, include pavement, grading, drainage, outdoor storage, and emergency access in the concept plan. Review flood mapping and site elevations with qualified professionals; neither vacant land nor an existing paved yard establishes that expansion is permissible.

- Grundy County Supervisor of Assessments : online assessment inquiry, forms, and Board of Review information.
- Grundy County Land Use Department : department structure and building-related starting points.
- Grundy County Planning and Zoning Office : hearing types and decision paths.

## Kane County: resolve multi-county names and construction scope

Geneva is a Kane County orientation point. Aurora and Elgin searches need particular care: both municipalities extend beyond Kane County. Find the actual county and municipal limits for the parcel before ordering records or estimating taxes. Kane's map directory supports municipality, address, and parcel research.

Kane County Building and Zoning provides property-research and permit instructions for unincorporated sites, including new construction, remodeling, repair, and demolition. Confirm whether a proposed equipment installation, mezzanine, dock alteration, or production conversion requires review; a prior tenant's permit is not approval for your project.

For operations whose routes cross the Fox River, test the specific crossing and local approach with the intended vehicle rather than relying on distance between towns. Check road authority, posted restrictions, and documented access rights. A mapped route does not establish legal truck access or a dependable delivery time.

- Kane County Supervisor of Assessments : parcel and assessment research for Kane County portions of a property.
- Kane County Building and Zoning Division : unincorporated property research, permit instructions, and references.
- Kane County maps : official entry point for parcel and municipality mapping.

## Kendall County: verify service authority and expansion assumptions

Yorkville and Oswego are useful municipal starting points for Kendall County searches. Check the specific parcel when a search reaches a county boundary; a municipal name is not a substitute for county identification. The county GIS department provides mapping resources for that investigation.

Kendall's Planning, Building and Zoning Department describes services for unincorporated areas and the incorporated villages of Millbrook and Plattville. This is a reason to confirm service arrangements rather than assuming that incorporation always rules out a county role. Ask which office handles each zoning, building, and inspection step for the address.

When evaluating land for a warehouse or a manufacturing expansion, request written utility availability, extension responsibilities, and the approvals for subdivision or site changes. Review the county's Land Resource Management Plan as planning context, then confirm current zoning and any required relief. Budget approvals and infrastructure separately from the advertised land price.

- Kendall County Supervisor of Assessments : assessment records, township assessor contacts, and appeals.
- Kendall County Planning, Building and Zoning : service area, land-use planning, and department guidance.
- Kendall County Geographic Information Systems : official mapping and property-information entry point.

## Lake County, Illinois: use early assistance for complex projects

Waukegan and Gurnee are Lake County, Illinois municipal examples. This section does not cover Indiana's Lake County or Wisconsin property. Lake County's permitting page directs incorporated-site inquiries to the village or city and describes county permits for unincorporated sites.

For a complicated nonresidential project in unincorporated Lake County, the county describes Early Assistance meetings coordinated across applicable county departments. Bring a specific site and an operational concept: a manufacturing process, a warehouse change of use, or a flex conversion needs more detail than a square-footage target.

The permitting page distinguishes change-of-use, site-development, building, conditional-use, and other approvals. Ask which apply to production, earthwork, outdoor activity, or a new storage arrangement. Use the county's mapping hub for initial geographic research, and verify drainage, wetland, and flood questions with the appropriate authority and specialists.

- Lake County, Illinois Chief County Assessment Office : assessment records, exemptions, and appeal procedures.
- Lake County Permits, Approvals and Early Assistance : unincorporated permitting and coordinated project guidance.
- Lake County, Illinois mapping and open data : official geographic-data starting point.

## McHenry County: combine land-use maps with permit history

Woodstock and Crystal Lake are municipal starting points within McHenry County. The county Planning and Development Department directs incorporated-site inquiries to the city or village; its permitting services apply to unincorporated areas.

The county GIS Interactive Maps directory distinguishes Athena property information from PlanDev zoning and land-use research. Read current zoning separately from proposed land use. For an existing industrial building, use the department's Electronic Records Search to investigate available closed permits and zoning petitions, then request missing records and confirmation of present approvals.

For distribution or storage uses, review the full route between the site and destinations, not just a regional highway label. Include local truck access, drainage, loading-hour constraints, and neighboring uses in the review. For a manufacturing conversion, reconcile the record history with the proposed equipment, wastewater, ventilation, and fire-protection needs.

- McHenry County Office of Assessments : assessment notices, parcel inquiry, and complaint deadlines.
- McHenry County Planning and Development : county permitting and land-use services.
- McHenry County GIS Interactive Maps : property and planning map directory.
- McHenry County Electronic Records Search : available permit and zoning records, not proof of current building condition.

## Will County: separate freight proximity from usable access

Romeoville is a Will County municipal example. Joliet searches can cross into Kendall County, so verify each parcel rather than assigning the entire city to Will. For incorporated sites, begin with the municipality; use county land-use staff for county-administered zoning questions.

Will County's Current Planning and Zoning section describes map amendments, special uses, variances, and building-permit zoning review. It maintains official zoning maps and records. Request the zoning district, relevant approvals, and any conditions affecting yards, parking, setbacks, or proposed activity; an industrial district label alone is not a project approval.

For a warehouse or distribution operation advertised near freight infrastructure, confirm the actual gate-to-destination route, terminal access arrangements where relevant, staging, queuing, and legal trailer parking. Nearby rail facilities do not mean a building has rail service or access rights. For manufacturing, investigate utility and process approvals independently of freight proximity.

- Will County Supervisor of Assessments : assessment records, exemptions, and appeal information.
- Will County Land Use Department : official department entry point.
- Will County Current Planning and Zoning : zoning applications, permit review, plans, and records.

## Match the operation in every county

- **Warehouse and storage**: Identify commodities, rack layout, storage height, slab loads, and fire-protection design. Verify usable clear height below obstructions and whether approved storage arrangements fit the inventory.
- **Distribution and logistics**: Model peak vehicle movements, dock appointments, truck turning, queuing, trailer storage, and employee access. Test routes at relevant times; neither county location nor highway proximity guarantees travel time.
- **Manufacturing**: Give reviewers equipment and process details, electrical demand, water use, discharge, emissions, noise, vibration, and operating hours. Confirm utility capacity and applicable permits before assuming an industrial building can accommodate production.
- **Flex space**: Define the office/industrial mix, customer visits, parking, occupancy classification, ventilation, and separation between uses. Existing office improvements do not establish permission for assembly, production, or storage.

Use the industrial building-fit checklist for measurements, systems, loading, and inspection questions. County research complements that checklist; it does not replace an engineer's, environmental professional's, or code specialist's review.

## Build a property-specific diligence file

- Identity and authority: retain the PINs, boundary evidence, zoning designation, responsible offices, and written responses about the exact use.
- Records and site risk: collect approvals, permit history, title and survey information, access rights, drainage documents, and tax records for every parcel. Use the correct county assessor and treasurer, not Cook County by default.
- Flood and environmental review: start with the FEMA Flood Map Service Center and EPA All Appropriate Inquiries guidance , then commission appropriate site-specific work. Maps and an assessment are not guarantees that all risk is absent.
- Cost and schedule: itemize improvements, utility upgrades, permit dependencies, and responsibility for ongoing maintenance. Use the leasing guide or purchase-diligence guide for transaction-specific questions.

Record the source, access date, parcel searched, verified finding, and unresolved question. Official pages and applications can change; if a map or portal is unavailable, contact the named county department. For the broader research process, see commercial property research .

> This hub is general education, not a listing service, market ranking, appraisal, or legal, tax, engineering, environmental, or investment advice. It makes no claim about available inventory, rents, returns, incentives, or professional credentials. Obtain property-specific advice and current source documents before making a commitment.

Owner guide · Illinois industrial tax diligence

# Property taxes on Illinois industrial real estate

A practical guide to how tax bills, reassessments, incentives, and lease pass-throughs affect small and midsize industrial assets in Illinois.

Educational, not tax or legal advice.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

## In brief
- Tax moves from assessment to equalization, levy, rate, bill, and collection.
- Cook uses classifications; collar counties generally follow the state assessment standard.
- For a sale, model the likely future bill, not only the seller’s current bill.
- Incentives, zones, and TIFs require document review.
- Leases should allocate appeals, refunds, escrows, and reassessment risk.
- Owner lens: An appeal does not itself stop tax bills, lender escrows, or lease pass-throughs. Budget the cash payment separately and calendar every filing, payment, and tenant reconciliation date.

_Industrial parcels in Elk Grove Village, Illinois. Verify parcel boundaries, PINs, assessments and tax districts in official records._

_National Park Service staff review plans at Cape Cod National Seashore. Organize your property’s tax evidence and deadlines using official county records._

## How Illinois property tax works at a high level

Industrial property taxes in Illinois are local taxes administered through a state-supervised system. The short version is assessment, equalization, levy, rate, bill, and collection. Each step should be checked against the parcel’s county, municipality, school district, and special districts.

### From assessment to bill
- **Assessment**: The assessor estimates taxable value. Outside Cook County, Illinois generally uses a statutory assessment level of 33⅓% of fair cash value before equalization and exemptions. Cook County applies its own classification levels.
- **Equalization**: An equalization factor, also called a multiplier, may adjust assessments so assessment levels are more uniform. See assessed value and equalization factor .
- **Levy**: Taxing districts adopt levies for schools, municipalities, counties, parks, libraries, fire, sanitary, and other local services.
- **Rate and extension**: The county clerk extends rates against equalized assessed value. The rate is not set by the assessor.
- **Bill and collection**: The county treasurer sends and collects the bill. Illinois property taxes are commonly paid after the tax year and in installments; confirm the exact calendar with the county treasurer.

## Cook County versus the collar counties

### Cook County classification

Cook County has an elected county assessor and assigns every PIN a classification code. The Cook County Assessor says classification determines the level of assessment, and its commercial valuation page states that office, industrial, and retail buildings typically have a 25% level of assessment . Residential and multifamily examples are different, which is why mixed-use and conversion assumptions need care.

Cook reassesses by region on a triennial cycle. The glossary definition of triennial reassessment is a reminder to check the current township calendar before relying on an old value.

### Collar-county assessment

In DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry, and Will counties, the initial local assessment commonly involves a township assessor with review by the county supervisor of assessments. The state guide describes the 33⅓% standard and equalization process; county pages provide the working deadlines and local forms.

## Reading an industrial tax bill

### Fields to review

**Common fields on an industrial tax bill**
- Field: Why it matters
- PIN or parcel number: Industrial sites may have multiple PINs for building, yard, parking, or excess land. Confirm all parcels transfer.
- Assessed value and EAV: Shows the assessment base before rates. Compare it with notices, appeals, and the assessor property card.
- Equalization factor: The multiplier can change the taxable base even when the local assessment appears unchanged.
- Exemptions: Industrial property usually has few owner exemptions; verify any exemption, incentive, or special assessment before assuming it continues.
- Taxing districts: School, municipal, county, park, fire, library, and special districts drive the combined rate.
- Tax rate and extensions: The rate converts EAV into the bill. High rates can change buyer proceeds and tenant pass-throughs.
- TIF notation: A TIF district can affect how incremental taxes are allocated and how incentives are documented.

## Reassessment, appeals and deadlines

Appeals are deadline-driven. A missed assessor, board of review, or state appeal date can shift the issue into a later tax year. Build a tax calendar during diligence instead of waiting for the bill.

### Appeal forums
- Assessor review: informal or formal review at the assessor level, depending on the county and township calendar.
- County Board of Review: county-level appeal after assessment publication. In Cook, the Cook County Board of Review has its own filing rules.
- State or court review: after the county level, an owner may evaluate the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board or circuit court with counsel.

### Evidence for industrial property

Industrial evidence usually focuses on the income approach, comparable sales, recent arms-length transactions, vacancy or functional issues, rent roll limits, deferred maintenance, environmental conditions, and building-specific constraints such as loading, clear height, sprinklers, power, or yard usability.

## Cook County incentive classifications for industrial property

Cook County has special incentive classes. The industrial incentive most often discussed is Class 6b , which the assessor describes as encouraging industrial development through new industrial facilities, rehabilitation of existing industrial structures, and industrial reutilization of abandoned buildings.

### Class 6b basics

The current Cook County Class 6b eligibility bulletin states the reduced assessment schedule is 10% for the first ten years, 15% in year eleven, and 20% in year twelve , subject to the ordinance and application requirements. Do not rely on the shorthand alone: review the application, municipal resolution, occupancy history, abandonment facts, renewal status, and compliance conditions.

### Incentive diligence questions

Confirm approval, transferability, renewal, municipal resolution, compliance conditions, and lease allocation of benefit, refunds, and appeal control.

## Enterprise zones and TIF districts

An enterprise zone is a designated area that may offer incentives if the project qualifies. Illinois DCEO says each zone has a local administrator and that a project seeking a building-material sales tax exemption certificate must contact that administrator. Eligibility is project-specific, not automatic.

A TIF district is different. A tax increment financing district can redirect eligible growth in tax revenue for public purposes within a district. It may appear on local maps, redevelopment agreements, or tax bills. In both cases, read the governing documents, expiration dates, and assignment rules.

## Taxes in underwriting and leases

### Lease controls
- NNN leases : confirm whether real estate taxes pass through, whether reassessment is included, and whether refunds are shared.
- Appeals: decide who may file, who pays professionals, and how settlements affect tenants.
- Escrows: lenders may require tax escrows; buyers should align closing prorations and lender reserves.
- Transfer taxes: Illinois, county, and municipal transfer taxes may apply. Chicago has its own finance department and rules. See transfer tax .

For sale-process context, see Illinois and Cook County considerations and pricing approach .

## A seller’s and buyer’s tax checklist

**Industrial property tax diligence checklist**
- Topic: Review
- Parcels: List every PIN and confirm against deed, survey, zoning lot, and operating site.
- Current taxes: Review bills, payment status, prorations, escrows, and delinquencies.
- Assessments: Compare notices, classifications, equalization factors, and reassessment scenarios.
- Appeals: Disclose open matters; verify deadlines, evidence, and lease refund clauses.
- Incentives: Confirm applications, ordinances, approvals, renewals, transferability, and clawbacks.
- Leases: Check pass-through, refund, contest, and reassessment language.

## How can an Illinois owner manage property taxes year-round?

Start with a parcel file: every PIN, property card, areas, use/classification, assessment notices, current and prior bills, leases, vacancy records and capital-condition evidence. Correct factual errors with the responsible office. An appeal addresses the assessment and evidence; the assessor does not set every taxing district's levy or guarantee a particular tax bill.

### Cook cycle versus filing windows

Cook reassesses each region once every three years, but appeal opportunities and changed-property reviews are not limited to the triennial mailing. Use the current township calendar for the actual notice and appeal dates; a building's town name alone is not the appeal deadline. Track the Board of Review window separately. In the collar counties, use the county assessment publication, local Board of Review rules and annual equalization information rather than importing Cook's cycle.

### Assessor, Board of Review and PTAB are different steps

Check local assessor review first where available, then the county Board of Review filing requirements. A PTAB appeal normally follows a Board of Review decision; PTAB's filing instructions describe a 30-day period and the applicable decision/notification rules, including Cook-specific transmittal information. Have counsel confirm the trigger, entity representation, current forms, evidence and alternatives before the deadline. PTAB recommends an appraisal for commercial and industrial appeals; unsupported asking prices are not the same evidence.

Build a calendar with the notice date, last filing date, evidence deadline, professional engagement, decision and any further-review deadline. Do not assume filing an appeal suspends tax payment obligations. Counsel and the treasurer should confirm payment and refund handling.

### Budget the bill and tenant allocation, not only an appeal result

Keep a documented base-case budget and a higher-tax scenario for reassessment, equalization, levies and incentive expiration. Do not book an unawarded appeal reduction as certain savings. Track accrued taxes, installments, lender escrow and closing prorations separately so the same bill is not counted twice.

Review recoverable tax definitions, caps, appeal fees, refund sharing and responsibility after a sale in each lease. A gross-lease owner can bear a tax increase that a net-lease owner partly recovers; an incentive benefit may flow to tenants. Update the NOI bridge and cash budget with both sides of that change.

## Class 6b, Class 7 and Class 8: which program fits?

The Cook County Assessor's incentive directory supplies the governing eligibility bulletins and application forms. A reduced assessment classification is not a grant or an automatic percentage reduction of the tax bill. Confirm municipal support, project eligibility, deadlines, continued use, ownership changes and compliance before underwriting it.

**Program purpose, not a determination of eligibility**
- Class: General purpose: Owner diligence
- 6b: Industrial development, rehabilitation and reutilization of qualifying abandoned industrial buildings: Industrial use, work/occupancy history, municipal resolution and remaining schedule
- 7a / 7b: Qualifying commercial projects in areas needing commercial development; project-cost and feasibility requirements distinguish the classes: Not a substitute industrial class; check the current bulletin's category and development-cost rules
- 8: Industrial/commercial development in qualifying areas experiencing severe economic stagnation: Area designation, project conditions and local support; not every Cook property qualifies

Model income and taxes with and without the incentive, especially at expiration or renewal. Approval, continuation and tenant recovery must be documented. Consult municipal staff, the Assessor and qualified tax counsel rather than describing a class as guaranteed savings.

## Illinois owner tax questions

### How can I lower commercial property taxes in Illinois?

Check parcel characteristics and assessment evidence, then file with the correct assessor or Board of Review within its calendar. Review further PTAB or court options with counsel. An assessment change does not guarantee a proportional tax-bill change because rates, levies and equalization also matter.

### Does a Cook County incentive transfer automatically on sale?

Do not assume it. Verify approval documents, the remaining schedule, ownership/use requirements and current renewal or compliance rules with the Assessor and municipality before pricing the benefit.

## Official sources

### State and regional sources
- Illinois Department of Revenue and Publication 136
- Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board
- Illinois DCEO Enterprise Zone Program
- City of Chicago Department of Finance

### Nine-county assessment offices

Assessment office links: Cook , DeKalb , DuPage , Grundy , Kane , Kendall , Lake , McHenry , and Will . Cook-specific billing and review sources: Treasurer and Board of Review .

> This guide is general education, not legal, tax, appraisal, accounting, brokerage, or investment advice. Property tax rules, assessment notices, appeal deadlines, incentives, and transfer taxes change. Verify the parcel, current year, office calendar, lease language, and transaction documents with qualified professionals before acting.

## Continue with the owner guides

For the operating and financial questions behind this decision:
- How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building
- How is net operating income calculated for commercial property?
- Commercial property owner questions: income, costs and decisions

Owner guide · Chicagoland industrial sale preparation

# Selling an industrial property in Chicagoland

This guide helps owners prepare a 10,000 to 100,000 square foot industrial property for sale in the nine-county Illinois market.

Educational, not a valuation or listing.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

## In brief

- Buyers often include owner-users, private investors, 1031 exchange buyers, and smaller institutional or fund buyers.
- Leased buildings are underwritten from income, term, credit, and expenses; vacant buildings from utility and financing fit.
- Value depends on function and risk: loading, clear height, systems, zoning, environmental history, leases, and deferred maintenance.
- A clean file and confidentiality plan can reduce diligence friction.
- Owner lens: Compare net proceeds, not just price: include debt payoff and prepayment costs, transaction expenses, tax planning, repair credits, and any leaseback rent and obligations.

_Industrial buildings in Elk Grove Village, Illinois. Regional illustration, not a listing or a transaction attributed to Pavlo Rospopa._

## Who buys this size range

Industrial assets between 10,000 and 100,000 square feet attract common buyer types. The audience depends on occupancy, function, location, financing, and timing.

- Owner-users: companies that want to occupy for warehouse, distribution, manufacturing, service, or flex operations.
- Private investors: local or regional buyers seeking income, vacancy upside, or long-term control.
- 1031 exchange buyers: investors using a tax-deferred exchange under IRC Section 1031.
- Small institutional or fund buyers: professional buyers focused on credit, scale, lease term, and repeatable industrial features.

A leased asset may appeal most to investors. A vacant asset may also draw owner-users that value control more than current income.

## How buyers underwrite

### Leased buildings

For a leased property, buyers start with the rent roll, lease documents, NOI, and the risk of keeping that income. They review lease term, WALT, tenant credit, options, expense recoveries, and landlord duties.

Recoveries matter because leases differ. A buyer will test whether taxes, insurance, CAM, repairs, management fees, and capital items pass through or remain with the owner.

### Vacant or owner-user buildings

For a vacant building, buyers focus on function, replacement cost, timing, financing, and needed improvements. Clear height, loading, power, office ratio, truck movement, and code compliance can matter more than a rent roll.

Owner-users may evaluate conventional financing and programs such as SBA 504 loans . Verify eligibility and terms with the SBA, a lender, and qualified advisors.

For building-fit questions, see the industrial building evaluation guide .

## What drives value in this segment

Value is not based on square footage alone. Buyers value buildings that solve a clear operating need.

**Common value drivers for 10,000 to 100,000 square foot industrial assets**
- Category: What buyers review
- Building function: Clear height, loading, truck court, columns, office percentage, floor plan, and expansion potential.
- Systems and condition: Roof, HVAC, slab, fire protection, lighting, docks, power, and deferred maintenance.
- Site and access: Outdoor storage, trailer parking, circulation, ingress, egress, utilities, and drainage.
- Legal and records: Zoning, permits, occupancy certificates, title, survey, easements, and environmental history.
- Income profile: Lease structure, rent, recovery language, obligations, remaining term, options, and credit.

The nine-county research hub helps identify parcel, zoning, and assessment offices.

## Preparing the document file

Organize documents before broad marketing. Missing records can slow offers, financing, title review, environmental review, and closing.

**Industrial property seller document checklist**
- Document: Why it matters
- Leases and amendments: Confirm rent, term, options, use, maintenance, and assignment terms.
- Rent roll: Summarizes tenants, spaces, rents, deposits, options, and dates.
- Estoppels and SNDAs: Support tenant and lender confirmation.
- Operating statements: Show two to three years of income, expenses, and recoveries.
- Tax bills and assessment notices: Support tax, appeal, and reassessment review.
- CAM reconciliations: Show common-cost billing and settlement.
- Phase I ESA and environmental reports: Identify environmental diligence and unresolved issues.
- ALTA survey and title commitment: Support review of boundaries, easements, and exceptions.
- Roof, HVAC, and fire-protection reports: Document condition, inspections, repairs, and recommended work.
- Warranties and service records: Support capital work, coverage, and maintenance claims.
- Permits and certificates of occupancy: Confirm approved work, occupancy, and use history.
- Zoning verification: Documents permitted uses, parking, storage, and constraints.
- Floor plans and site plan: Show layout, docks, office area, yard, parking, and access.
- Service contracts: Show snow, landscaping, security, waste, maintenance, and utilities.
- Environmental and regulatory records: Cover permits, tanks, spills, notices, and closure documents.

## Physical preparation before marketing

Physical preparation should make the site easier to inspect.

- Address obvious deferred maintenance where practical, or price and disclose it.
- Clean warehouse areas, mechanical rooms, offices, loading areas, and yard.
- Replace missing lighting, repair trip hazards, and label key electrical or utility areas.
- Organize roof, HVAC, dock, fire-protection, and paving records for recent capital work.
- Confirm what personal property, racks, equipment, and fixtures are included or excluded.

For leased buildings, coordinate site access with the tenant. A clean tour process protects operations and informs buyers.

## Pricing approach

A broker opinion of value is a marketing and pricing opinion, not a formal appraisal. An appraisal is prepared for a defined purpose, standard, date, and client.

For leased industrial property, buyers often discuss cap-rate math. Conceptually, NOI divided by a capitalization rate indicates value before deal-specific adjustments.

> Illustration only, not market data. If placeholder NOI is $300,000 and the placeholder cap rate is 6.0%, the arithmetic is $300,000 ÷ 6.0% = $5,000,000. Actual value depends on property-specific income, risk, lease terms, building condition, financing, and current buyer demand.

For vacant or owner-user property, pricing may be tested against sales, replacement cost, renovation cost, timing, and alternatives.

## Typical sale process

Sale processes vary. This sequence is not a promise of timing or outcome.

- Prep: gather records, resolve open questions, set pricing strategy, and define confidentiality rules.
- Marketing or confidential offering: present the asset to targeted buyers with controlled information release.
- Tours: coordinate buyer access, tenant notice, operations, and safety requirements.
- Offers and LOI: compare price, deposits, contingencies, diligence, closing conditions, and buyer credibility.
- PSA negotiation: document the purchase agreement, representations, closing obligations, remedies, and timelines.
- Due diligence and inspection period: buyers review leases, title, survey, zoning, environmental, physical, and financial records.
- Financing contingency: if applicable, lenders review collateral, borrower strength, leases, appraisal, environmental reports, and title.
- Closing: finalize conditions, funds, deeds, prorations, notices, possession, and post-closing obligations.

The commercial investment diligence guide explains buyer-side items sellers should anticipate.

## Illinois and Cook County considerations

Cook County reassesses real property on a triennial cycle. Confirm current assessment status, appeal periods, and property-specific records with the Cook County Assessor .

Transfer taxes may apply at state, county, and municipal levels. Verify current requirements with official sources such as the Illinois Department of Revenue and, for Chicago property, the City of Chicago Department of Finance .

Do not rely on quoted rates from old closing statements or summaries. Municipal rules and exemptions can be property-specific, and parties should verify obligations before signing a purchase agreement.

## Sale-leaseback and 1031 exchange planning

### Sale-leaseback

An owner-user can sometimes sell the property and lease it back from the buyer. This may free capital while keeping the business in place, but it turns the seller into a tenant with lease obligations.

Buyers will underwrite rent, lease term, renewal options, maintenance duties, credit, and the business's ability to keep paying rent. The lease should be negotiated with the same care as the sale.

### 1031 exchange planning

A seller considering a 1031 exchange should plan before closing. Under IRC Section 1031, the identification period is 45 days and the exchange period is 180 days, subject to statutory rules and details.

Use a qualified intermediary and tax advisor. Start with the IRS and confirm the structure, deadlines, related-party rules, replacement property, and documentation before relying on exchange treatment.

## Confidentiality with tenants and employees

Confidentiality matters when a building is occupied or when an owner-user is still operating. Buyers need information, but tenants and employees may react to rumors before facts are available.

- Decide what information is public, what requires a signed confidentiality agreement, and what waits until a serious buyer is qualified.
- Limit tenant contact unless lease review, estoppels, tours, or lender diligence require it.
- Schedule tours around operations, safety rules, and sensitive business areas.
- Prepare a communication plan for employees if the business occupies the property.

Confidentiality should not be used to conceal material issues. It should control process, protect operations, and keep information accurate.

## Thinking about selling?

I specialize in the investment sales of industrial assets from 10,000 to 100,000 square feet across Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry, and Will counties. If you would like a second opinion on a building or on timing, reach out.

Connect on LinkedIn Marcus & Millichap advisor page

> This guide is general education, not legal, tax, engineering, environmental, appraisal, brokerage, or investment advice. Verify property records, taxes, zoning, environmental matters, loan programs, and transaction documents with qualified professionals before acting.

## Planning an industrial property exit for retirement

Compare holding with professional management, selling for liquid proceeds and a qualifying 1031 exchange before choosing a retirement date. Estimate cash after loan payoff, sale costs and taxes, and test lease rollover, major capital work and refinancing risk. If your company occupies the building, coordinate the business sale and future lease separately.

The retirement exit guide explains why a 1031 exchange is not an IRA rollover, how retaining a building changes your workload and concentration, and which questions to bring to tax, financial and estate advisers.

Before closing, review depreciation recapture and the sale gain example and lazy 1031 and DST exchange choices . Mortgage payoff changes sale cash, not ordinarily taxable gain, and less management can bring fees, restricted liquidity and sponsor risk.

## Continue with the owner guides

For the operating and financial questions behind this decision:
- How is net operating income calculated for commercial property?
- How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building
- Commercial property owner questions: income, costs and decisions
- Retirement planning with commercial real estate
